title: Regional steering and failover operational notes
content:
Purpose:

Quick working notes on regional traffic steering approaches we should evaluate for Redwood's public control plane and Dedicated/Private deployments. Focus is on combining GeoDNS, Anycast, and control-plane routing policies so we can support: regional affinity, low-latency routing, controlled failover, and cross-region load smoothing. This is an operational sketch — assumptions, tradeoffs, open questions and a migration sketch.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Primary plan: use DNS-based region preference (GeoDNS) for initial affinity + BGP Anycast for global ingress where we control egress/edge (hosted API + public endpoints).
- Control plane exposes region weights and override flags (canary, emergency-redirect).
- Health checks + global health aggregation service drive automatic failover and region demotion.
- Short TTLs for GeoDNS (30s–60s) for faster steering; also support long TTLs with an active push channel for Dedicated customers who prefer stability.

Motivation and constraints:
- Customers require predictable latency, regional data residency options, and graceful degradation.
- Hosted API must be low-latency across NA/EU/APAC. Private deployments may not let us run Anycast edges inside their VPC; design must accommodate that.
- We must minimize user-visible churn during background autoscaling events while still enabling quick failover when a region is impaired.

Steering primitives considered:
1) GeoDNS (region preference + weighted answers)
   - Pros: easy to implement with Route53/Cloud DNS, per-region weights, can be combined with latency-based routing.
   - Cons: DNS caches, client resolver behavior (EDNS/EDNS client subnet), inconsistent geo lookups, and propagation delays.

2) Anycast (BGP) fronting + edge regionalization
   - Pros: fast failover (BGP withdraws), consistent IP for customers, good for streaming/long-lived connections.
   - Cons: requires controlling many edge locations, BGP complexity, not viable inside private customer networks.

3) Client-side routing hints (client sends preferred_region header)
   - Pros: deterministic when client SDKs follow policy; good for Dedicated where we can push SDK changes.
   - Cons: relies on client version adoption.

4) Control-plane routing (central decision service + redirect/302, or token-based routing)
   - Pros: precise and fast switching; ability to implement canaries and gradual rollouts.
   - Cons: adds an extra hop/latency if implemented synchronously; increases control-plane coupling.

Recommended hybrid design:
- Public endpoints (hosted API): Anycast + regional backend mapping
  - Deploy Anycast IPs in colocations / cloud edge POPs. Edge does quick health checks to local region pools. If local pool degraded, edge routes to a secondary region pool via internal tunnel (GRE/VPN) or sends 302 redirect to region-specific hostname.
  - Control plane publishes per-region weight and a small set of region-to-backend mappings to edges. Edges fetch policy via secure API and apply locally.
  - Use DNS to advertise region-specific hostnames for direct region targeting (e.g., eu.api.redwood.com -> eu-backend set). DNS remains the fallback mechanism for non-Anycast clients.

- Dedicated & Private customers:
  - Prefer DNS + client routing hints. For Dedicated networks where we operate egress, offer optional Anycast. For Private VPCs, provide a control-plane managed routing policy that customer can pull (or we push via config/CloudFormation).

Key control plane responsibilities:
- Central policy store: region weights, active canaries, emergency override flags, TTL recommendations, and per-customer routing policies.
- Health aggregation service: roll up region health from SRE probes, edge reports, and customer-reported telemetry. Emit region_state: healthy/degraded/down and reason.
- Audit log & RBAC: every change to steer policy must be auditable.
- Push / pull sync: edges must be able to pull latest policy; urgent changes push via webhook/WSS to reduce DNS reliance.

Health check model and failover logic:
- Multi-layer checks: internal infra (autoscaler, queue depth), model serving health (GRPC ping), and SLO signals (p99 latency, error rate).
- Health aggregation rules: if region has >X% internal failures OR p99 latency > target for Y minutes, mark degraded. If degraded AND sustained for Z minutes, demote region weight by configurable factor and trigger traffic redistribution.
- On full outage, mark region down and withdraw from Anycast / remove from DNS answer sets.

DNS details and TTL strategy:
- Default TTL = 60s for geo records. For regions with sensitive clients (financial/regulatory), allow static mappings with TTL = 3600s and an explicit change protocol.
- DNS answers contain multiple IPs: prefer local-region IP first, then cross-region fallbacks. Weighted answers used for smooth migration.
- Monitor resolver behavior: track EDNS/EDNS-Client-Subnet; if client resolvers ignore EDNS, fall back to latency-based routing via monitoring data.

Anycast behavior specifics:
- Edge nodes hold a small policy cache. For flows that need region affinity (e.g., chat sessions), edge can sticky-route based on session token -> consistent hashing into region pool.
- For long-poll/streaming connections, avoid DNS-based rebalancing; prefer transparent edge failover (local buffering + internal redirection) to avoid broken streams.

Operational playbooks (high-level):
1) Partial region degradation (gradual): control plane automatically shifts weight 70/30 -> 50/50 over 10 minutes, with SRE alerting and rollback window.
2) Sudden region outage: mark region down, withdraw Anycast advertisements, remove DNS answers, push emergency override to edges to stop routing. Create incident, open customer comms.
3) Canary rollout: start with region weight 5% for new model, monitor quality and cost metrics for 60–120 minutes, automate rollback if quality regression triggers.

Migration plan (phased):
- Phase 1 (proof): implement control-plane policy store + health aggregator. Wire into current DNS provider to update weighted Geo records. Pilot with one region pair (us-east / us-west).
- Phase 2 (edge pilot): deploy edge policy sync to a subset of Anycast POPs (partners/colos). Test edge-driven routing decisions and 302 fallback behavior.
- Phase 3 (scale): full Anycast rollout for hosted API, provide Dedicated feature toggles, document Private deployment constraints.

Metrics to track:
- User-visible: median latency, p95/p99, connection success rate, streaming drop rate after failover.
- Control-plane: policy propagation latency (time between change and edge/apply), DNS answer update time, health aggregation lead/lag.
- Cost: cross-region egress delta, extra CPU for proxying fallback traffic.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- TTL vs propagation speed: what fraction of customers depend on long DNS caches? Do we need a long-lived push channel for Dedicated?
- Anycast ownership: should we partner with a provider (Cloudflare/NS1/CloudFront) or operate our own BGP in key POPs? (Cost + ops delta).
- Per-customer override granularity: allow customer-level pinned regions vs global control-plane. Security and audit implications.
- Upstream resolver behavior: how many important customers are behind resolvers that ignore EDNS? Need concrete telemetry.

Immediate action items (who/when):
- [Maya] implement policy store schema draft and open spec doc (due 2025-11-30).
- [Arjun] instrument DNS resolver telemetry in hosted API (due 2025-12-08).
- [Lena] prototype edge policy sync proto and failure modes (due 2026-01-15).
- [SRE] define health aggregation thresholds and alerting playbooks (due 2025-12-20).

Appendix — quick ASCII flow for runtime decisioning:

Client -> DNS resolves api.redwood.com -> returns [local-edge-anycast-ip, eu-backend-ip]
Client -> connects to Anycast IP at edge A
Edge A pulls policy and local health -> sees local region healthy -> forward to local pool
Edge A detects pool degraded -> if tunnel available -> route to backup region via internal link; else -> return 302 to client pointing to region-specific hostname (eu.api.redwood.com) and mark session for tracing

Notes / caveats:
- 302 redirect approach is for short-term compatibility; ideally edge-level transparent failover is preferred to avoid broken clients.
- For Dedicated customers that want strict data locality, control plane must support pinned-only routing with manual override process (no automatic demotion unless customer consents).

End of notes — keep this doc as living draft and iterate after pilots.

Unresolved items to surface in design review:
- exact thresholds for health demotion (X/Y/Z above),
- telemetry schema for policy propagation latency,
- test harness for simulated cross-region outages (chaos tests).
